items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Like Coleman Hawkins. Like Bunny Berigan. Like Benny Goodman, Chu Berry, Dizzy Gillespie. They all had a sound that they could be recognized.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: To me, the originator, like Coleman Hawkins, is just as great as Thomas Edison... I think he was the most influential, more than Coleman Hawkins, more than anybody that I know of right now.

ctx.x: Why don't they give him the credit while he's living, while he's originating, like they do a Thomas Edison? To me, the originator, like Coleman Hawkins, is just as great as Thomas Edison, to me. To me he is because in his field he originated something on the tenor saxophone, you know.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I’m going out of town with Coleman Hawkins.

ctx.x: How did he get his musical interest? Where did that come from? Seems he would be so occupied with making a living on the farm, that….did he work professionally?

He was a coal miner. And everyone there was a coal miner. And he used to listen to records. I think Bessie Smith was the most popular one there. And Mamie Smith. And I got interested in one that Louis Armstrong made with Bessie Smith. He made quite a few I think, him and Earl Hines and Coleman Hawkins. And that attracted my attention, and I began to listen to Louis Armstrong and from then on after I heard him play on these records I had no doubt in my mind I was going to try and be a trumpet player. I still am.…
